Use the photograph to answer the question.

This 1936 Farm Security Administration photograph by Arthur Rothstein shows a desolate farmstead on the Great Plains. A father and his two sons run toward their small wooden farmhouse as a massive wall of dust approaches from behind. The land around the house is flat and barren, with drifting dust partially burying fences and farm structures.

(Photograph by Arthur Rothstein for the Farm Security Administration, 1936. Library of Congress, Farm Security Administration Collection.)

How did agricultural farming practices of the early twentieth century contribute to the environmental disaster shown in this photograph?

Farmers over-planted forests, cutting off wind patterns that normally brought rainfall to the plains region

Mechanized farming had also accelerated the scale of this land conversion. Choice A describes a problem in a different region. Choice C reverses the causal relationship. Choice D confuses the water-related Dust Bowl with different agricultural practices.

items.stem: The Scopes Trial of 1925 pitted high school teacher John Scopes against the state of Tennessee for teaching evolution in violation of the Butler Act. Clarence Darrow defended Scopes, and William Jennings Bryan prosecuted. Though Scopes was found guilty and fined, Bryan's credibility was severely damaged during cross-examination. What does the trial's outcome reveal about the relationship between legal verdicts and broader cultural conflicts?
items.stemEs: El Juicio Scopes de 1925 enfrentó al maestro de secundaria John Scopes contra el estado de Tennessee por enseñar la evolución en violación de la Ley Butler. Clarence Darrow defendió a Scopes, y William Jennings Bryan lo acusó. Aunque Scopes fue declarado culpable y multado, la credibilidad de Bryan fue severamente dañada durante el contrainterrogatorio. ¿Qué revela el resultado del juicio sobre la relación entre los veredictos legales y los conflictos culturales más amplios?

choices.text: The conviction of Scopes demonstrated that religious fundamentalism had permanently defeated scientific modernism in American public life.
choices.textEs: La condena de Scopes demostró que el fundamentalismo religioso había derrotado permanentemente al modernismo científico en la vida pública estadounidense.

choices.text: Scopes was acquitted, demonstrating that courts would protect scientific teaching from religious censorship.
choices.textEs: Scopes fue absuelto, demostrando que los tribunales protegerían la enseñanza científica de la censura religiosa.

choices.text: A legal verdict can be technically won while the broader cultural argument is lost, as Bryan's defeat in public opinion represented a symbolic victory for modernism despite Scopes's conviction.
choices.textEs: Un veredicto legal puede ganarse técnicamente mientras se pierde el argumento cultural más amplio, ya que la derrota de Bryan en la opinión pública representó una victoria simbólica para el modernismo a pesar de la condena de Scopes.

choices.text: The Scopes Trial immediately resulted in the repeal of anti-evolution laws across the United States, ending the conflict over teaching Darwin in public schools.
choices.textEs: El Juicio Scopes resultó inmediatamente en la derogación de las leyes anti-evolución en todo los Estados Unidos, poniendo fin al conflicto sobre la enseñanza de Darwin en las escuelas públicas.

items.explanation: The Scopes Trial shows that a legal verdict can be technically irrelevant to the cultural conflict it represents — Scopes was convicted but modernist scientific thinking won the broader public debate, as Bryan's literal fundamentalism was exposed as intellectually vulnerable. The trial became a symbolic defeat for anti-evolution forces despite the legal outcome. C captures this divergence between legal outcome and cultural significance. A conflates the legal verdict with cultural outcome. B misrepresents the verdict — Scopes was convicted. D is factually inaccurate; the Butler Act remained in force in Tennessee until 1967.

items.stem: The Scopes Trial has often been portrayed as a simple conflict between science and religion, with urban modernists versus rural fundamentalists. Historians have challenged this simplified narrative, noting that William Jennings Bryan was also a Populist who had championed workers and farmers, and that his objection to evolution was partly rooted in concerns about Social Darwinism's use to justify inequality. How does this context complicate the standard interpretation of the Scopes Trial?
items.stemEs: El Juicio Scopes ha sido frecuentemente retratado como un simple conflicto entre la ciencia y la religión, con modernistas urbanos frente a fundamentalistas rurales. Los historiadores han cuestionado esta narrativa simplificada, señalando que William Jennings Bryan también fue un populista que había defendido a los trabajadores y agricultores, y que su objeción a la evolución estaba parcialmente arraigada en preocupaciones sobre el uso del Darwinismo Social para justificar la desigualdad. ¿Cómo complica este contexto la interpretación estándar del Juicio Scopes?

choices.text: The context confirms the standard interpretation: the trial was simply a conflict between ignorant rural fundamentalism and enlightened urban science.
choices.textEs: El contexto confirma la interpretación estándar: el juicio fue simplemente un conflicto entre el fundamentalismo rural ignorante y la ciencia urbana ilustrada.

choices.text: Bryan's Populist background reveals that he was actually sympathetic to racial equality and used the trial to challenge segregationist uses of evolutionary theory.
choices.textEs: El trasfondo populista de Bryan revela que en realidad era simpatizante de la igualdad racial y usó el juicio para desafiar los usos segregacionistas de la teoría evolutiva.

choices.text: Bryan's Populist background reveals that he secretly opposed the prosecution of Scopes but was forced by political pressure to lead the anti-evolution case.
choices.textEs: El trasfondo populista de Bryan revela que secretamente se oponía al procesamiento de Scopes pero fue obligado por la presión política a liderar el caso anti-evolución.

choices.text: Bryan's opposition to evolution was partly motivated by concerns about Social Darwinism's use to justify inequality, revealing the trial as a conflict over competing social values, not merely religion versus science.
choices.textEs: La oposición de Bryan a la evolución estaba parcialmente motivada por preocupaciones sobre el uso del Darwinismo Social para justificar la desigualdad, revelando el juicio como un conflicto sobre valores sociales en competencia, no meramente religión versus ciencia.

items.explanation: The historical context reveals that the Scopes Trial was not simply science vs. religion, but also involved debates about what scientific theories justified — Bryan feared that Darwinian evolution, as applied to society, could be used to legitimize economic exploitation and racial hierarchy. D captures this complexity. A is the standard simplified narrative this question challenges. B misrepresents Bryan's actual positions on segregation, which were not notably progressive. C conflates Bryan's economic Populism with opposition to the trial itself, which he supported vigorously.
items.explanationEs: El contexto histórico revela que el Juicio Scopes no fue simplemente ciencia contra religión, sino que también involucró debates sobre qué justificaban las teorías científicas: Bryan temía que la evolución darwiniana, aplicada a la sociedad, pudiera usarse para legitimar la explotación económica y la jerarquía racial. D captura esta complejidad. A es la narrativa simplificada estándar que esta pregunta desafía. B malinterpreta las posiciones reales de Bryan sobre la segregación, que no eran notablemente progresistas. C conflate el Populismo económico de Bryan con la oposición al juicio en sí, que apoyó vigorosamente.

choices.text: Media attention at the Scopes Trial ensured that the scientific arguments for evolution were clearly communicated to a national audience, permanently shifting public opinion toward modernism.

items.stem: The Scopes Trial legacy persists in American culture: debates about evolution in public school curricula continued throughout the 20th century and into the 21st century. What conclusion about American political culture does the long-term persistence of this debate most strongly support?
items.stemEs: El legado del Juicio Scopes persiste en la cultura americana: los debates sobre la evolución en los planes de estudio de las escuelas públicas continuaron a lo largo del siglo XX y hasta el siglo XXI. ¿Qué conclusión sobre la cultura política estadounidense apoya más fuertemente la persistencia a largo plazo de este debate?

choices.text: Conflicts between science and religion in American public life are inevitable and will always end with science eventually winning decisive legal victories.
choices.textEs: Los conflictos entre la ciencia y la religión en la vida pública estadounidense son inevitables y siempre terminarán con la ciencia ganando eventualmente victorias legales decisivas.

choices.text: Curriculum debates in public education often serve as proxy conflicts over deeper questions of community identity, values, and who controls the socialization of the next generation.
choices.textEs: Los debates sobre el plan de estudios en la educación pública a menudo sirven como conflictos proxy sobre preguntas más profundas de identidad comunitaria, valores y quién controla la socialización de la próxima generación.

choices.text: The persistence of evolution debates is purely a regional Southern phenomenon, reflecting that region's cultural isolation from national scientific consensus.
choices.textEs: La persistencia de los debates sobre la evolución es puramente un fenómeno regional sureño, que refleja el aislamiento cultural de esa región del consenso científico nacional.

choices.text: The ongoing debate demonstrates that the scientific community has never reached consensus about the validity of evolutionary theory.
choices.textEs: El debate en curso demuestra que la comunidad científica nunca ha alcanzado consenso sobre la validez de la teoría evolutiva.

items.explanation: The enduring Scopes debate demonstrates that in American political culture, conflicts over public education curriculum are proxy battles for deeper conflicts over community identity, values, and authority — questions about who controls the socialization of children and what worldview public institutions should transmit. B correctly identifies this proxy-conflict dynamic. A presents an unsupported deterministic claim about inevitable resolution. C misrepresents the issue as purely regional when it was national. items.stem: The scientific and cultural debate during the Scopes Trial reflected a broader tension between empiricism (knowledge through evidence and observation) and revelation (knowledge through religious authority and scripture). In the trial, both sides appealed to different epistemological frameworks. What does this epistemological conflict reveal about the nature of the 1920s modernity debate?
items.stemEs: El debate científico y cultural durante el Juicio Scopes reflejó una tensión más amplia entre el empirismo (conocimiento a través de la evidencia y la observación) y la revelación (conocimiento a través de la autoridad religiosa y las escrituras). En el juicio, ambos lados apelaban a diferentes marcos epistemológicos. ¿Qué revela este conflicto epistemológico sobre la naturaleza del debate sobre la modernidad en la década de 1920?

choices.text: The trial was fundamentally about whether evolution was scientifically correct, with both sides ultimately agreeing that the empirically superior explanation should win.
choices.textEs: El juicio trató fundamentalmente sobre si la evolución era científicamente correcta, con ambos lados acordando en última instancia que la explicación empíricamente superior debería ganar.

choices.text: The trial revealed a conflict over which knowledge system — scientific empiricism or religious revelation — should hold authority over public truth claims, particularly in the socialization of children through public education.
choices.textEs: El juicio reveló un conflicto sobre qué sistema de conocimiento — el empirismo científico o la revelación religiosa — debería tener autoridad sobre las afirmaciones de verdad pública, particularmente en la socialización de los niños a través de la educación pública.

choices.text: The trial definitively resolved the conflict between science and religion by establishing a legal principle that scientific explanations must always supersede religious ones in public settings.
choices.textEs: El juicio resolvió definitivamente el conflicto entre la ciencia y la religión estableciendo un principio legal de que las explicaciones científicas siempre deben reemplazar a las religiosas en entornos públicos.

choices.text: Both Bryan and Darrow agreed that scientific and religious knowledge were compatible, but disagreed only about whether evolution was actually supported by the scientific evidence available in 1925.
choices.textEs: Tanto Bryan como Darrow estaban de acuerdo en que el conocimiento científico y religioso eran compatibles, pero solo discrepaban sobre si la evolución estaba realmente respaldada por la evidencia científica disponible en 1925.

items.explanation: The Scopes epistemological conflict reveals that the 1920s modernization debate was not simply about specific facts (did humans evolve from earlier primates?) but about which knowledge system — scientific empiricism or religious revelation — should have authority over public truth claims, especially in public education. B captures this deeper authority-of-knowledge conflict. A reduces the conflict to a factual dispute when it was fundamentally about authority and epistemology. C makes a false empirical claim about the trial's legal outcome with respect to a different issue. D misrepresents the historical positions; Bryan explicitly argued for biblical authority rather than the compatibility of both frameworks.
items.explanationEs: El conflicto epistemológico de Scopes revela que el debate sobre la modernización de la década de 1920 no era simplemente sobre hechos específicos (¿evolucionaron los humanos de primates anteriores?) sino sobre qué sistema de conocimiento — el empirismo científico o la revelación religiosa — debería tener autoridad sobre las afirmaciones de verdad pública, especialmente en la educación pública. B captura este conflicto más profundo sobre la autoridad del conocimiento. A reduce el conflicto a una disputa fáctica cuando era fundamentalmente sobre autoridad y epistemología. C hace una afirmación empírica falsa sobre el resultado legal del juicio con respecto a un problema diferente. D malinterpreta las posiciones históricas; Bryan argumentó explícitamente a favor de la autoridad bíblica en lugar de la compatibilidad de ambos marcos.

items.stem: Between 1920 and 1929, technological change, consumer culture, racial conflict, immigration restriction, and religious-scientific tension all developed simultaneously and interactively. A historian argues that these trends were not independent developments but aspects of a single underlying process. What is the most defensible characterization of that underlying process?
items.stemEs: Entre 1920 y 1929, el cambio tecnológico, la cultura del consumidor, el conflicto racial, la restricción de la inmigración y la tensión religiosa-científica se desarrollaron simultáneamente e interactivamente. Un historiador argumenta que estas tendencias no eran desarrollos independientes sino aspectos de un único proceso subyacente. ¿Cuál es la caracterización más defendible de ese proceso subyacente?

choices.text: Rapid modernization disrupted existing social hierarchies, cultural authorities, and community identities simultaneously, generating both liberation for those empowered by change and organized resistance from those threatened by it.
choices.textEs: La rápida modernización perturbó las jerarquías sociales existentes, las autoridades culturales y las identidades comunitarias simultáneamente, generando tanto liberación para quienes fueron empoderados por el cambio como resistencia organizada de quienes se sintieron amenazados por él.

choices.text: All 1920s social conflicts were caused exclusively by economic inequality — if wealth had been distributed more equally, racial conflict, immigration restriction, and religious controversy would not have occurred.
choices.textEs: Todos los conflictos sociales de la década de 1920 fueron causados exclusivamente por la desigualdad económica: si la riqueza se hubiera distribuido de manera más equitativa, el conflicto racial, la restricción de la inmigración y la controversia religiosa no habrían ocurrido.

choices.text: All major 1920s social conflicts were imported from Europe through immigration, and native-born Americans would have achieved a peaceful, progressive society without foreign influence.
choices.textEs: Todos los principales conflictos sociales de la década de 1920 fueron importados de Europa a través de la inmigración, y los estadounidenses nacidos en el país habrían logrado una sociedad pacífica y progresista sin influencia extranjera.

choices.text: The underlying process was pure social decline — every development of the 1920s represented a moral and social deterioration with no genuinely positive dimensions.
choices.textEs: El proceso subyacente fue un puro declive social: cada desarrollo de la década de 1920 representó un deterioro moral y social sin dimensiones genuinamente positivas.

items.explanation: All the major 1920s social conflicts can be understood as expressions of a single underlying tension: the rapid modernization of American economy and society disrupted existing social hierarchies, cultural authorities, and community identities, generating both celebration from those empowered by change and resistance from those threatened by it. This modernization-disruption framework connects the Scopes Trial, Klan revival, immigration restriction, Harlem Renaissance, and consumer culture as related responses to the same structural transformation. A captures this synthetic explanatory framework. B presents a single-cause explanation that is too narrow. C presents a false empirical claim about external causation. D presents an overly pessimistic and unsupported claim about purely negative effects.
items.explanationEs: Todos los principales conflictos sociales de la década de 1920 pueden entenderse como expresiones de una única tensión subyacente: la rápida modernización de la economía y la sociedad estadounidenses perturbó las jerarquías sociales existentes, las autoridades culturales y las identidades comunitarias, generando tanto celebración de quienes fueron empoderados por el cambio como resistencia de quienes se sintieron amenazados por él. Este marco de modernización-disrupción conecta el Juicio Scopes, el resurgimiento del Klan, la restricción de la inmigración, el Renacimiento de Harlem y la cultura del consumidor como respuestas relacionadas a la misma transformación estructural. A captura este marco explicativo sintético. B presenta una explicación de causa única que es demasiado estrecha. C presenta una afirmación empírica falsa sobre la causación externa. D presenta una afirmación excesivamente pesimista y sin apoyo sobre efectos puramente negativos.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from the transcript of State of Tennessee v. John T. Scopes (Rhea County Circuit Court, Dayton, Tennessee, July 1925), during Clarence Darrow's cross-examination of William Jennings Bryan, July 20, 1925 (trial transcript, public domain, Library of Congress collection):

"DARROW: Do you think the earth was made in six days?
BRYAN: Not six days of twenty-four hours.
DARROW: Doesn't it say so?
BRYAN: No, sir…
DARROW: What do you think?
BRYAN: I do not think about things I don't think about.
DARROW: Do you think about things you do think about?
BRYAN: Well, sometimes."

This exchange took place in Dayton, Tennessee, during the trial of high school teacher John T. Scopes, who was charged with violating the Butler Act (Tennessee's law banning the teaching of evolution). Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Scopes Trial (US.31) and the broader cultural divisions of the 1920s (US.33, US.34), write a 1–2 paragraph CER response that claims what the Scopes Trial revealed about the tensions between modernity and traditionalism in 1920s America. Support your claim with specific evidence from the excerpt and from your knowledge, and reason through why this trial in a small Tennessee town became a national event.
items.stemEs:
Lee el siguiente extracto de la transcripción del caso Estado de Tennessee contra John T. Scopes (Tribunal de Circuito del Condado de Rhea, Dayton, Tennessee, julio de 1925), durante el contrainterrogatorio de Clarence Darrow a William Jennings Bryan, 20 de julio de 1925 (transcripción del juicio, dominio público, colección de la Biblioteca del Congreso):

"DARROW: ¿Cree usted que la tierra fue creada en seis días?
BRYAN: No en seis días de veinticuatro horas.
DARROW: ¿No es eso lo que dice?
BRYAN: No, señor…
DARROW: ¿Qué piensa usted?
BRYAN: No pienso en cosas sobre las que no pienso.
DARROW: ¿Piensa en cosas sobre las que sí piensa?
BRYAN: Bueno, a veces."

Este intercambio tuvo lugar en Dayton, Tennessee, durante el juicio del maestro de secundaria John T. Scopes, quien fue acusado de violar la Ley Butler (la ley de Tennessee que prohibía la enseñanza de la evolución). Usando este extracto y tu conocimiento del Juicio Scopes (US.31) y las divisiones culturales más amplias de los años 1920 (US.33, US.34), escribe una respuesta CER de 1 a 2 párrafos que afirme qué reveló el Juicio Scopes sobre las tensiones entre la modernidad y el tradicionalismo en la América de los años 1920. Apoya tu afirmación con evidencia específica del extracto y de tu conocimiento, y razona por qué este juicio en un pequeño pueblo de Tennessee se convirtió en un evento nacional.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score response will: (1) Claim—e.g., 'The Scopes Trial in Dayton, Tennessee, exposed the deep cultural fault line between scientific modernity and religious fundamentalism that defined 1920s America, becoming a national media spectacle precisely because both sides recognized the trial as a proxy battle for the nation's identity.' Read the following three primary source excerpts and answer the prompt below.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT A
Tennessee Butler Act, Chapter 27, House Bill 185, enacted March 21, 1925 (Tennessee Acts, 64th General Assembly, public domain):

"An Act prohibiting the teaching of the Evolution Theory in all the Universities, Normals and all other public schools of Tennessee, which are supported in whole or in part by the public school funds of the State, and to provide penalties for the violations thereof. Be it enacted by the General Assembly of the State of Tennessee, That it shall be unlawful for any teacher in any of the Universities, Normals and all other public schools of the State which are supported in whole or in part by the public school funds of the State, to teach any theory that denies the story of the Divine Creation of man as taught in the Bible, and to teach instead that man has descended or ascended from a lower order of animals."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT B
Scopes Trial transcript, cross-examination of William Jennings Bryan by Clarence Darrow, Rhea County Circuit Court, Dayton, Tennessee, July 20, 1925 (public domain, Library of Congress):

"DARROW: Do you think the earth was made in six days?
BRYAN: Not six days of twenty-four hours.
DARROW: Doesn't it say so?
BRYAN: No, sir…I do not think about things I don't think about.
DARROW: Do you think about things you do think about?
BRYAN: Well, sometimes.
[Laughter from the crowd.]"

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT C
H.L. Mencken, "Homo Neanderthalensis," Baltimore Sun, July 29, 1925 (pre-1928 publication, public domain):

"Such is the great capital of the Fundamentalists, such is the Athens of the Coca-Cola belt. What could be more lovely?…The yokels have been galvanized. They leap and cavort. They roll and cry. They are led by a prophet who knows all the answers. Bryan is their Moses and their Woodrow Wilson."

─────────────────────────────────────────
Using ALL THREE documents and your knowledge of the Scopes Trial (US.31), cultural changes of the 1920s (US.33), and mass media (US.34), write a multi-paragraph response that applies HIPP to each document and constructs an argument about what the Scopes Trial revealed about 1920s American culture. Be sure to identify each document's purpose and point of view, explain what the three together show that no single document shows alone, and use outside knowledge to support your argument. Note: This trial took place in Dayton, Tennessee — identify what the Tennessee context adds to your analysis.
items.stemEs:
Lee los siguientes tres extractos de fuentes primarias y responde al ejercicio.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO A

"Un acto que prohíbe la enseñanza de la Teoría de la Evolución en todas las Universidades, Normales y todas las demás escuelas públicas de Tennessee, que son sostenidas total o parcialmente por los fondos de las escuelas públicas del Estado, y para establecer penas por las violaciones del mismo. Sea promulgado por la Asamblea General del Estado de Tennessee, Que será ilegal para cualquier maestro en cualquiera de las Universidades, Normales y todas las demás escuelas públicas del Estado que son sostenidas total o parcialmente por los fondos de las escuelas públicas del Estado, enseñar cualquier teoría que niegue la historia de la Creación Divina del hombre según se enseña en la Biblia, y enseñar en cambio que el hombre ha descendido o ascendido de un orden inferior de animales."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO B
Transcripción del Juicio Scopes, contrainterrogatorio de William Jennings Bryan por Clarence Darrow, Tribunal de Circuito del Condado de Rhea, Dayton, Tennessee, 20 de julio de 1925 (dominio público, Biblioteca del Congreso):

BRYAN: No en seis días de veinticuatro horas.
DARROW: ¿No es eso lo que dice?
BRYAN: No, señor…No pienso en cosas sobre las que no pienso.
DARROW: ¿Piensa en cosas sobre las que sí piensa?
BRYAN: Bueno, a veces.
[Risas de la multitud.]"

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO C
H.L. Mencken, "Homo Neanderthalensis", Baltimore Sun, 29 de julio de 1925 (publicación anterior a 1928, dominio público):

"Tal es la gran capital de los Fundamentalistas, tal es la Atenas del cinturón de Coca-Cola. ¿Qué podría ser más hermoso?…Los lugareños han sido galvanizados. Saltan y se agitan. Ruedan y lloran. Son liderados por un profeta que conoce todas las respuestas. Bryan es su Moisés y su Woodrow Wilson."

Asegúrate de identificar el propósito y punto de vista de cada documento, explica qué muestran los tres juntos que ningún documento muestra solo, y usa conocimiento externo para apoyar tu argumento. Nota: Este juicio tuvo lugar en Dayton, Tennessee — identifica qué añade el contexto de Tennessee a tu análisis.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score response (6/6) will: (1) HIPP on Document A: Historical context—1920s rural Tennessee, fundamentalist religious revival; Intended audience—Tennessee citizens and legislators; Purpose—legislate religious belief into public education, protect traditional values from secular science; Point of view—rural, Protestant legislative majority using state power to enforce religious orthodoxy. (2) HIPP on Document B: Historical context—seventh day of trial, moved outdoors due to crowds; Intended audience—packed courthouse and, via telegraph/newspaper, national audience; Purpose—Darrow uses Bryan's own words to expose the inconsistency of Biblical literalism; Point of view—urban secular attorney using Socratic questioning to discredit fundamentalism in the court of national opinion. (3) HIPP on Document C: Historical context—post-trial reporting; Intended audience—Northern urban readership; Purpose—ridicule fundamentalism and Southern rural culture; Point of view—elite Northern journalist deploying condescension that itself reveals urban-rural cultural contempt. (4) Together: the three documents show the trial as a media event—the law (A) was the legal trigger, the courtroom (B) was the dramatic content, and the press (C) was the national amplifier. (5) Tennessee context: Dayton's business leaders actually invited the ACLU to use the town for the test case, hoping for tourism revenue—illustrating how the trial served multiple agendas simultaneously. (6) Outside evidence: ACLU sponsorship, radio coverage, Scopes convicted and fined $100, Bryan's death five days later, Butler Act not repealed until 1967.

items.stem: The Scopes Trial of 1925 in Dayton, Tennessee centered on a state law that:

choices.text: Prohibited the teaching of evolution in public schools
Required public schools to teach the theory of evolution
Required all public school students to attend religious services
Banned the teaching of any science in public schools

items.explanation: The 1920s saw deep cultural conflict: Prohibition reflected traditionalist influence; the Scopes Trial dramatized the evolution-religion divide; immigration quotas (1924) reflected nativist backlash; and the KKK resurged targeting Catholics, Jews, and immigrants. These culture wars shaped American politics for decades.

items.stem:
Read the following two primary source excerpts and answer the prompt below.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT A
William Jennings Bryan, closing statement prepared for the Scopes Trial, Dayton, Tennessee, 1925 (Bryan never delivered this statement — the trial ended before the defense rested — but it was published posthumously in Memoirs of William Jennings Bryan, 1925, public domain):

"The real issue is not what is true in science, but whether teachers paid by the taxpayers shall be permitted to undermine the religious faith of the children of those taxpayers… I am not making any argument against the truth of evolution. I am arguing against the right of evolutionists to demand pay for teaching that which is offensive to those who pay the taxes."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT B
Clarence Darrow, closing argument in the Scopes Trial, Rhea County Circuit Court, Dayton, Tennessee, July 1925 (trial transcript, public domain, Library of Congress):

"If today you can take a thing like evolution and make it a crime to teach it in the public schools, tomorrow you can make it a crime to teach it in the private schools, and next year you can make it a crime to teach it to the hustings or in the church. At the next session you may ban books and the newspapers. Ignorance and fanaticism are ever busy and ever in need of fresh victories. Whenever they are stopped they must be stopped or they will pile on ignorance upon ignorance and fanaticism on fanaticism, until we shall all find ourselves in the very darkness of the middle ages."

─────────────────────────────────────────
Both of these arguments were made in Dayton, Tennessee during the 1925 Scopes Trial. Using BOTH documents and your knowledge of the Scopes Trial (US.31) and cultural tensions of the 1920s (US.33), write a multi-paragraph response that applies HIPP to each document and constructs an argument about the fundamental values in conflict at the Scopes Trial and why this conflict mattered beyond Dayton, Tennessee. Your response must analyze each document using all four HIPP elements, explain what each author believed was truly at stake, and use outside knowledge to assess the lasting significance of this Tennessee trial for American constitutional history.
items.stemEs:
Lee los siguientes dos extractos de fuentes primarias y responde al ejercicio.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO A
William Jennings Bryan, declaración de cierre preparada para el Juicio Scopes, Dayton, Tennessee, 1925 (Bryan nunca pronunció esta declaración —el juicio terminó antes de que la defensa descansara— pero fue publicada póstumamente en Memorias de William Jennings Bryan, 1925, dominio público):

"El verdadero problema no es qué es verdad en la ciencia, sino si se permitirá a los maestros pagados por los contribuyentes minar la fe religiosa de los hijos de esos contribuyentes… No argumento contra la verdad de la evolución. Argumento contra el derecho de los evolucionistas a exigir pago por enseñar lo que ofende a quienes pagan los impuestos."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO B
Clarence Darrow, alegato final en el Juicio Scopes, Tribunal de Circuito del Condado de Rhea, Dayton, Tennessee, julio de 1925 (transcripción del juicio, dominio público, Biblioteca del Congreso):

"Si hoy puedes tomar algo como la evolución y hacerlo delito enseñarlo en las escuelas públicas, mañana puedes hacerlo delito enseñarlo en las escuelas privadas, y el año que viene puedes hacerlo delito enseñarlo en los mítines o en la iglesia. En la próxima sesión puedes prohibir libros y periódicos. La ignorancia y el fanatismo siempre están activos y siempre necesitan nuevas victorias. Cuando se los detiene, deben detenerse o acumularán ignorancia sobre ignorancia y fanatismo sobre fanatismo, hasta que todos nos encontremos en la oscuridad más profunda de la Edad Media."

─────────────────────────────────────────
Ambos argumentos se hicieron en Dayton, Tennessee durante el Juicio Scopes de 1925. Usando AMBOS documentos y tu conocimiento del Juicio Scopes (US.31) y las tensiones culturales de los años 1920 (US.33), escribe una respuesta de varios párrafos que aplique HIPP a cada documento y construya un argumento sobre los valores fundamentales en conflicto en el Juicio Scopes y por qué este conflicto importó más allá de Dayton, Tennessee. Tu respuesta debe analizar cada documento usando los cuatro elementos HIPP, explicar qué creía cada autor que estaba verdaderamente en juego, y usar conocimiento externo para evaluar la importancia duradera de este juicio de Tennessee para la historia constitucional americana.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score response (6/6) will: (1) HIPP on Document A: Historical context—Bryan's position as champion of rural Protestant fundamentalism; Intended audience—his prepared remarks are to the jury and public record; Purpose—reframe the trial from science vs. religion to taxpayer rights vs. elite imposition, avoiding the science question; Point of view—populist Democratic politician who made his career championing ordinary people; limitation—Bryan retreats from defending Biblical literalism to defending community control, revealing that the cross-examination had damaged his credibility. (2) HIPP on Document B: Historical context—Darrow speaking in a court where the verdict was predetermined (Scopes was convicted); Intended audience—national public via press (Darrow knew the trial had become a media event); Purpose—make the case for academic freedom and warn against the slippery slope of legislating belief; Point of view—secular humanist attorney whose real audience is history, not the Rhea County jury. (3) What each author saw at stake: Bryan saw local democratic control over publicly funded education; Darrow saw the First Amendment and the entire architecture of intellectual freedom. (4) National significance: Butler Act not repealed until 1967; Epperson v. Arkansas (1968) SCOTUS ruling; creation-evolution debate continues into the 21st century; establishes the 'culture war' template for American politics. (5) Outside evidence: ACLU's role, Mencken's press coverage, radio broadcast, Bryan's death, conviction upheld on appeal.

items.stem: The 1920s have been described as a decade when 'modern America' and 'traditional America' came into direct conflict. The Scopes Trial in Dayton, Tennessee became the most visible symbol of this conflict. Using your knowledge of the Scopes Trial (US.31), Jazz Age cultural changes (US.33), and the rise of mass media (US.34), write an extended essay that argues whether the 1920s cultural conflict between modernity and traditionalism was primarily a regional divide (urban North vs. rural South) or a deeper national struggle over values. Your essay must: (1) state a clear, defensible claim about the nature of the conflict; (2) use specific evidence from all three standards; (3) address how mass media transformed a local Tennessee trial into a national event; and (4) synthesize across the standards to assess the long-term legacy of this conflict for American cultural and political life. Your essay should be 4–6 well-developed paragraphs. Be sure to address the significance of the Tennessee setting specifically.

El Juicio Scopes en Dayton, Tennessee se convirtió en el símbolo más visible de este conflicto. Usando tu conocimiento del Juicio Scopes (US.31), los cambios culturales de la Era del Jazz (US.33) y el surgimiento de los medios masivos (US.34), escribe un ensayo extendido que argumente si el conflicto cultural de los años 1920 entre la modernidad y el tradicionalismo fue principalmente una división regional (Norte urbano vs. Sur rural) o una lucha nacional más profunda sobre los valores. Tu ensayo debe: (1) formular una afirmación clara y defendible sobre la naturaleza del conflicto; (2) usar evidencia específica de los tres estándares; (3) abordar cómo los medios masivos transformaron un juicio local en Tennessee en un evento nacional; y (4) sintetizar a través de los estándares para evaluar el legado a largo plazo de este conflicto para la vida cultural y política americana. Tu ensayo debe tener 4–6 párrafos bien desarrollados. Asegúrate de abordar específicamente la importancia del contexto de Tennessee.

(2) Evidence from all three standards — US.31: Butler Act (Tennessee), ACLU sponsorship, Darrow vs. Bryan, Scopes convicted, Bryan's death five days after trial, Butler Act not repealed until 1967; US.33: Jazz Age as the cultural expression of modernity that fundamentalism opposed — jazz labeled 'immoral,' flapper culture, Prohibition as parallel traditionalist backlash; US.34: radio broadcasting the Scopes Trial nationally; H.L. Arkansas (1968); creation science and intelligent design movements; school curriculum battles continue — the Scopes Trial established the template for American 'culture wars' that persisted through the 20th and into the 21st century.
